items.title: 10.10.1 Finding the charge on 1 mole of electrons

source_refs.note: Topic 10.10.1 with Figure 10.2, printed page 223. The printed apparatus drawing is not reproduced.

blocks.text: The charge on 1 mole of electrons is found from a simple electrolytic experiment with the apparatus of Figure 10.2. A pure copper anode and a pure copper cathode are weighed separately and arranged for the electrolysis of aqueous copper(II) sulfate. A variable resistor keeps the current constant at about 0.2 amperes, and a constant current is passed for a measured time, for example 40 minutes. The cathode and anode are removed, washed and dried with distilled water and then with propanone, and reweighed. The cathode gains mass because copper is deposited; the anode loses mass because copper goes into solution as copper ions. The decrease in the mass of the anode is measured, because copper does not always stick to the cathode well.

blocks.caption: The experiment
rows: pure copper anode and cathode, weighed before and after
about 0.2 A, kept constant with a variable resistor, for a measured time
loss of mass of the anode (copper dissolves as Cu2+)

blocks.prompt: Why is the loss in mass of the anode preferred to the gain of the cathode, and why are the electrodes rinsed with propanone?
blocks.explanation: Deposited copper can be loose and flake off the cathode, so its gain is unreliable, whereas the anode loses exactly the copper that dissolved. Propanone displaces the water and evaporates quickly, so the electrodes dry without heating and are weighed without residual water.

items: Weigh copper electrodes; electrolyse CuSO4(aq) at a constant 0.2 A for a measured time; wash with water and propanone, dry and reweigh; use the anode's loss of mass.
